lesson.title: SACK: Telling the Sender Exactly What Arrived
lesson.summary: The Selective Acknowledgment option lets a TCP receiver report specific non-contiguous blocks of data it has successfully received, so the sender can retransmit precisely what is missing instead of guessing.
lesson.body:
Plain TCP acknowledgments are cumulative, reporting only the highest byte number received in order, with no way to describe data that arrived out of order beyond a gap. This is exactly what makes fast retransmit's duplicate-ACK signal work, but it also means the sender, even after fast retransmit fires, has limited information about the true shape of the loss. If a single segment was lost from a window, cumulative ACKs are enough to figure out that one segment needs resending. But if two or more segments are lost from the same window, plain cumulative acknowledgment cannot easily tell the sender which specific segments are missing versus which ones actually arrived out of order and are sitting safely in the receiver's buffer. Left with cumulative ACKs alone, a sender recovering from multiple losses in one window either has to retransmit conservatively, resending things that may have already arrived, or recover slowly, discovering and fixing one loss per round trip.

The Selective Acknowledgment option, defined in RFC 2018 and commonly called SACK, solves this by letting the receiver report more than just the cumulative ACK point. Using extra space in the TCP options field, a receiver can list specific additional blocks of data, described as a starting and ending sequence number, that it has received and buffered even though they are not yet contiguous with the cumulative ACK point. This is a direct application of selective repeat thinking at the transport layer: rather than treating everything past a gap as needing retransmission the way a simple go-back-N approach would, SACK gives the sender a precise map of what the receiver actually has, so only the true gaps need to be resent.

Because TCP options space is limited, a single SACK block set typically reports up to three or four discontiguous ranges per ACK, which is normally more than enough to describe the pattern of loss within one window. The sender maintains a picture of which segments have been selectively acknowledged and uses that picture to decide exactly what to retransmit, skipping over ranges that SACK has already confirmed as received. This is a considerable improvement over inferring loss purely from duplicate ACK counts, especially as window sizes grew large enough that multiple losses within a single window became common on real, busy networks.

Consider a sender that transmits segments 1 through 10 in one window, and segments 3 and 7 are lost while everything else arrives. Without SACK, the receiver can only cumulatively acknowledge up through segment 2 no matter how much later data has arrived, leaving the sender to guess how much needs resending once duplicate ACKs indicate a problem. With SACK enabled, the receiver's ACKs continue to cumulatively acknowledge byte 2, but they now also carry SACK blocks reporting that segments 4 through 6 and segments 8 through 10 have already been received. The sender reads those blocks and immediately knows precisely two things are missing: segment 3 and segment 7, retransmitting exactly those two rather than resending segment 4 through 10 out of caution or discovering the second loss only after a slow, separate round of duplicate ACKs. In this way SACK does not replace fast retransmit, cumulative acknowledgment, or the congestion control decisions made by algorithms like Reno or CUBIC, it sharpens the information those mechanisms have to work with, letting recovery from multiple losses in a single window happen in close to one round trip instead of several.
